featured.title: Micron Heads Into Earnings With a Memory Shortage So Tight Even Apple Is Flinching
featured.excerpt: Sanjay Mehrotra's company has become the AI boom's quiet kingmaker. For NRIs, the story runs from a Gujarat fab to the price of the next iPhone.
featured.image_caption: Micron Technology chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra, photographed in 2025
featured.nri_angle: Micron's Indian-origin CEO is building a $2.75 billion assembly plant in Gujarat, and the same memory crunch lifting his stock is about to raise prices on every device Indian American families buy.
featured.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: Three Tankers, 94 Indian Sailors, and a Strait That Tried to Trap Them. They Finally Got Out.
news.excerpt: As the first oil cargoes move again through the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S.–Iran ceasefire, the slow release of 94 Indian crew on three tankers is a reminder of who actually keeps the world's energy moving — and who pays the price when the chokepoint closes.
news.image_caption: An oil tanker at sea; three Indian-flagged tankers carrying 94 crew cleared the Strait of Hormuz this week
news.nri_angle: India supplies more than 300,000 of the world's seafarers — a largely working-class diaspora whose remittances sustain families back home and whose labour moves a fifth of the world's oil through the Strait of Hormuz; the release of 94 Indian crew on three tankers, after others were stranded and three were killed, shows how directly the Gulf crisis lands on Indian families.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: A Box of Alphonsos Now Costs as Much as Lobster. The War in the Gulf Is Part of the Reason.
news.excerpt: Indian mango season in America has become a full-blown diaspora frenzy — WhatsApp alerts, warehouse runs, $2,000 'mango passes.' But this year the Strait of Hormuz crisis has pushed airfreight costs up, even as a new hybrid variety, Sonpari, makes its U.S. debut at $70 a box.
news.image_caption: Alphonso mangoes from India; diaspora demand has pushed premium boxes to lobster-tier prices in the U.S.
news.nri_angle: Indian mango season has become a beloved summer ritual for the U.S. diaspora — a $40 box as 'a plane ticket home' — but the Strait of Hormuz war has pushed up the airfreight these delicate, must-fly fruit depend on, even as a new hybrid, Sonpari, debuts at $70 a box, tying the price of nostalgia directly to Gulf geopolitics.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: Citizenship Was Supposed to Be the Finish Line. The Justice Department Is Quietly Reopening Old Files.
news.excerpt: A ramped-up federal denaturalization effort — a dedicated DOJ unit, a June memo listing ten priority categories, and a fresh batch of cases including the first in Oregon this term — is unsettling naturalized Indian-Americans who assumed the oath was the end of the immigration road, not a document the government could revisit.
news.image_caption: A U.S. naturalization ceremony; a ramped-up DOJ effort is reopening the question of whether citizenship is final
news.nri_angle: A sharply expanded federal denaturalization effort — a dedicated DOJ unit expecting 'several hundred' cases, a June memo listing ten priority categories, and the first Oregon case of the term targeting an Indian-origin man — is unsettling the roughly two million naturalized Indian-Americans who treated the citizenship oath as the irreversible end of their immigration journey.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: An Emergency-Room Doctor From Minneapolis Is About to Become the Diaspora's Newest Astronaut. Liftoff Is July 14.
news.excerpt: Anil Menon — son of a Malayali father and a Ukrainian mother, SpaceX's first flight surgeon, and now a U.S. Space Force colonel — will launch aboard Soyuz MS-29 for an eight-month stay on the International Space Station, adding another Indian-origin name to the short, storied list of those who have left the planet.
news.image_caption: NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who launches to the International Space Station aboard Soyuz MS-29 on July 14
news.nri_angle: Anil Menon — the Minneapolis-born son of a Malayali father and Ukrainian mother, SpaceX's first flight surgeon and now a U.S. Space Force colonel — launches July 14 aboard Soyuz MS-29 for an eight-month ISS mission, adding another Indian-origin name to the lineage of Kalpana Chawla, Sunita Williams and Shubhanshu Shukla and giving the diaspora a rare moment of pride beyond the daily churn of immigration and trade news.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: For the First Time in Six Years, Indians Are the Most Deported Nationality From Canada
news.excerpt: Canada removed 1,712 Indian citizens in the first quarter of 2026 — nearly a third of all deportations — and a record 6,980 Indian cases now sit in the removal queue, a sharp signal of how far the welcome mat has been pulled back for the country's largest immigrant community.
news.image_caption: Toronto's skyline; Indians are now the largest nationality deported from Canada in 2026
news.nri_angle: Indians are Canada's largest immigrant, student and temporary-worker community, so the country becoming its top deported nationality in 2026 — with a record 6,980 cases still pending removal — directly raises the stakes for hundreds of thousands of Indian families to track permit deadlines and file renewals early before a lapsed status hardens into a multi-year re-entry ban.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: The Gulf's Oil Is Flowing Again Through Hormuz. India Is in No Rush to Go Back.
news.excerpt: With two months of crude already in tank and Russian barrels still cheap, Indian refiners are letting Middle Eastern suppliers wait — even as the war's legacy lingers in a record import bill and four straight hikes at the pump that diaspora families feel on every trip home.
news.image_caption: A crude oil tanker; India is letting Gulf suppliers wait even as the Strait of Hormuz reopens
news.nri_angle: India's strategy after the Hormuz reopening — staying on cheap Russian crude rather than rushing back to Gulf suppliers — directly shapes the rupee, the trade deficit and pump prices, the everyday inflation NRIs feel on remittances and every trip home after India absorbed a record energy bill and four fuel-price hikes during the war.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: The UAE Just Gave Stranded Residents One Last Window. For Indians Caught by the Spring Airspace Chaos, the Clock Runs to July 9.
news.excerpt: Abu Dhabi's identity authority has opened a final 30-day grace period — running June 10 to July 9 — for those who benefited from this spring's overstay-fine waivers, letting them regularise their status or leave penalty-free as the Gulf's largest Indian community sorts out paperwork left in limbo by the regional flight shutdowns.
news.image_caption: Abu Dhabi's skyline; the UAE has opened a final 30-day visa grace period running to July 9, 2026
news.nri_angle: Indians are the UAE's largest expatriate community — over 3.5 million people — and many were left with lapsed or cancelled visas when regional airspace closed this spring; the ICP's final 30-day grace period to July 9, 2026 gives them a penalty-free path to either fix their status or leave, with a five-day consular service blackout (June 26–30) complicating the timeline.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: The Fed Just Hinted Its Next Move Is Up, Not Down. For NRIs, That Quietly Rewrites the Math on the Rupee and Their Dollar Savings.
news.excerpt: In Kevin Warsh's debut meeting the Federal Reserve held rates but flipped its dot plot toward a 2026 hike — firming the dollar, pressuring the rupee, and reshaping the calculus for diaspora investors weighing US yields against India's newly sweetened NRI deposit rates.
news.image_caption: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, whose first meeting signalled rates could rise in 2026
news.nri_angle: The Fed's hawkish turn under new Chair Kevin Warsh — a dot plot now pointing to a 2026 hike — strengthens the dollar and pressures the rupee, reshaping the trade-off NRIs face between elevated US yields and India's newly uncapped NRI deposit rates near 7 percent, and affecting the rupee value of every remittance sent home.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: India's Two Biggest Green-Card Doors Just Slammed Shut Until October. The July Visa Bulletin Spells It Out.
news.excerpt: The State Department's July 2026 Visa Bulletin marks EB-2 and EB-5 (unreserved) for India as 'Unavailable' and retrogresses EB-1 India by two months — a fiscal-year freeze that strands tens of thousands of skilled Indian professionals just weeks before the annual reset.
news.image_caption: A U.S. green card; the July 2026 Visa Bulletin marks EB-2 and EB-5 for India as 'Unavailable'
news.nri_angle: The July 2026 Visa Bulletin marks EB-2 and EB-5 (unreserved) for India as 'Unavailable' and retrogresses EB-1 India — freezing the green-card lanes that tens of thousands of Indian engineers, doctors and researchers rely on until the fiscal-year reset on October 1, 2026.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: Germany Just Made Layovers Easier for Indian Travellers. Lufthansa Thinks That Changes the Map to America.
news.excerpt: As of June 3, Indian passport holders no longer need a Schengen airport transit visa to change planes at Frankfurt or Munich — a quiet bureaucratic win that the Lufthansa Group now expects to redraw how the diaspora flies between India, the UK and the Americas.
news.image_caption: Frankfurt Airport, a key transit hub for Indian travellers, where transit visas are no longer required
news.nri_angle: Germany scrapped the Schengen airport transit visa for Indian passport holders effective June 3, 2026 — sparing students, professionals and families changing planes at Frankfurt or Munich the cost and paperwork of a Type A visa, and prompting Lufthansa to expect higher India traffic on routes to the UK and the Americas.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.excerpt: After a paper leak forced India to cancel 2.3 million NEET results, the medical entrance exam is being re-run on June 21 — with every overseas centre closed and Telegram blocked nationwide to stop cheating rackets.
news.image_caption: Families and guardians wait outside an entrance-examination centre in India as candidates sit the test.

news.title: The India-UK Trade Deal Finally Has a Date — and a Quiet Win for NRI Pay Packets
news.excerpt: CETA and the Double Contribution Convention both take effect July 15. The tariff cuts grabbed the headlines, but the clause that exempts 75,000 Indian professionals from UK National Insurance for five years is the one diaspora workers will feel.
news.image_caption: PM Narendra Modi receives UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in Mumbai, October 2025.

news.excerpt: A halted 81-foot Ram statue and a desecrated idol have pushed Bangladesh's anxious Hindu minority into the streets — and pulled India, Washington and the diaspora into the fight over their safety.
news.image_caption: A Durga Puja procession by members of Bangladesh's Hindu minority community in Dhaka.

news.title: India's Pilots Reject the AI171 'Suicide' Verdict. Their Simulator Says the Plane Failed, Not the Crew.
news.excerpt: The Federation of Indian Pilots says new tests show the official four-second timeline is 'physically impossible' — and points to a catastrophic electrical failure on the London-bound Boeing 787 that killed 241.
news.image_caption: Air India Boeing 787-8 VT-ANB, the aircraft that operated Flight AI171, at London Heathrow.

sources.label: Madhyamam / IANS — 'Electric failure led to Air India Boeing crash in Ahmedabad: Pilots’ body' (June 19, 2026)
ANI — 'Fuel switches moved without input, points to possible glitch: Federation of Indian Pilots Chief on AI171 crash report' (July 13, 2025)
The Sun — 'My wife died in the Air India crash… these questions need to be answered' (whistleblower electrical-failure evidence, June 2026)
Wikipedia — 'Air India Flight 171' (AAIB investigation timeline, EAFR recovery)

news.nri_angle: AI171 was a London-bound flight full of British-Indian and NRI passengers, and the diaspora flies the same Boeing 787 fleet weekly — so whether the crash is blamed on dead Indian pilots or a systemic Dreamliner flaw is a question with direct personal stakes.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: America's Tech Jobs Are Quietly Moving to Bengaluru. India's 'Capability Center' Workforce Is Nearing 2.4 Million.
news.excerpt: As Washington tightens the H-1B route, US firms like N-able are opening Global Capability Centers in India and hiring frontier AI and cybersecurity talent on Indian soil — the mirror image of the visa fight.
news.image_caption: International Tech Park in Whitefield, Bengaluru, a hub of India's Global Capability Center industry
news.nri_angle: The GCC boom rewrites the migration calculus for the diaspora: the cutting-edge job for an American company is increasingly available in Bengaluru or Hyderabad, without the visa lottery or green-card backlog — meaning a homecoming no longer has to be a career sacrifice.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: India's Women Open Their World Cup With a 95-Run Demolition — and the Diaspora Has a Home Tournament in England
news.excerpt: Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma powered India to 209 against the Netherlands at Headingley before the bowlers sealed a crushing win, as the 2026 Women's T20 World Cup unfolds across British-Indian heartlands.
news.image_caption: India opener Smriti Mandhana, whose batting anchors the side at the 2026 Women's T20 World Cup
news.nri_angle: A Women's T20 World Cup staged across England puts India's rising women's side within reach of one of the world's largest Indian diasporas — a rare home tournament for British-Indian fans and a source of role models for diaspora daughters taking up the game from Southall to Sunnyvale.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: India Is Heading for Its Weakest Monsoon in 11 Years. The Bill Will Land on Dinner Tables — Including the Diaspora's.
news.excerpt: A strengthening El Niño has left the 2026 monsoon delayed and deficient, with the IMD forecasting the lowest rainfall since 2015, Mumbai rationing water, and coffee, sugar and pulse crops already at risk.
news.nri_angle: A failing monsoon stokes food inflation and pushes New Delhi toward rice and sugar export curbs — the moves that spike basmati and onion prices in diaspora grocery stores abroad — while pressuring the rupee and the returns NRIs earn on Indian deposits, and threatening the incomes of relatives still farming back home.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

news.title: The $100,000 H-1B Fee Is Back. Indian Tech Workers Who Celebrated Its Defeat Have 72 Hours of Whiplash to Show for It.
news.excerpt: A Boston judge struck down the fee on June 8, then paused his own order on June 12 — so as of June 17 the $100,000 charge is again in force, with conflicting rulings in three courts pointing toward the Supreme Court.
news.image_caption: The Boston skyline; a federal judge in Boston struck down the H-1B fee on June 8, then paused his own order four days later
news.nri_angle: Nearly three-quarters of H-1B visas go to Indians, so a reinstated $100,000 fee threatens the principal on-ramp for Indian engineers, doctors and researchers — and the on-again, off-again legal whiplash forces diaspora families, students and physicians to make irreversible decisions against a rule that can flip in 72 hours.
news.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: An Award-Winning Indian Kitchen Is Opening in a Phoenix Mall. That's a Bigger Deal Than It Sounds.
nri-world.excerpt: NADU, a James Beard semifinalist and Michelin Bib Gourmand winner from Chicago, debuts at Desert Ridge — the latest sign that Indian food in America has stopped apologizing.
nri-world.image_caption: Tandoori chicken plated with herb rice in a modern fine-dining presentation, reflecting a new wave of regional Indian cooking in America.
nri-world.nri_angle: For a generation of Indian-Americans who grew up faintly embarrassed by the strip-mall curry house, the rise of regional Indian fine dining is a marker of cultural arrival — food that no longer asks permission to exist in America.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: After Three Temples Were Hit in Two Weeks, Hindu Americans Are Done Quietly Repainting the Walls
nri-world.excerpt: The Hindu American Foundation has formally asked California's hate commission to count anti-Hindu bias — a sign of a diaspora that has decided to be counted.
nri-world.image_caption: The BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir in Robbinsville, New Jersey, at sunset — one of the landmark Hindu temples built by the American diaspora.
nri-world.nri_angle: A community that long preferred private success to public advocacy is now writing letters to the state, lodging diplomatic complaints, and installing security cameras — formally demanding recognition among the communities at risk.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: America's Oldest Indian Association Swore In a New Board. The Guest List Was a Map of How Far the Community Has Come.
nri-world.excerpt: Founded in 1967 to get Indians counted on the U.S. census, the AIA now draws letters from senators and ambassadors — and faces a generational handover.
nri-world.image_caption: A community honoree holds an award before an applauding audience, a scene familiar at Indian-American organizational galas.
nri-world.nri_angle: The endless circuit of diaspora galas serves a real function: it is the connective tissue binding the founders who fought for census recognition to a second generation that no longer needs the organization for survival.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: A Doctor Born to Immigrants Is About to Spend Eight Months in Orbit. The Diaspora Has a New Kind of Hero.
nri-world.excerpt: Anil Menon, son of an Indian father and a Ukrainian mother, launches next month on his first spaceflight — a quiet rebuke to anyone who thinks the immigrant story has only one script.
nri-world.image_caption: NASA astronaut Anil Menon in his official portrait at the Johnson Space Center
nri-world.nri_angle: Menon's path — Harvard, Stanford, the ER, SpaceX, now the ISS — is the diaspora's familiar overachiever arc bent toward an unfamiliar destination. He represents a generation of Indian-American children no longer choosing between medicine and a dream.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: He Wore No. 10 for New Zealand and Made History for India Without Ever Playing for It
nri-world.excerpt: Sarpreet Singh became the first player of Indian heritage to start a World Cup match. He is one of at least four at this tournament — a scattered, accidental Indian team playing under other flags.
nri-world.image_caption: Sarpreet Singh training with FC Bayern Munich in 2019
nri-world.nri_angle: India has never qualified for a men's World Cup, yet its bloodlines are all over the 2026 tournament — in New Zealand, Australian, Qatari and Congolese shirts. It is the diaspora's strange consolation: present everywhere, representing no one back home.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: India Dangled a 7% Dollar Return at the Diaspora. Now Its Banks Are Scrambling to Fund the Promise.
nri-world.excerpt: The RBI's special deposit window could pull in $55-70 billion from NRIs by September. But behind the headline rates, banks are quietly fighting over who is allowed to make the loans that make the math work.
nri-world.image_caption: An aerial view of GIFT City, India's tax-neutral financial hub in Gandhinagar, Gujarat
nri-world.nri_angle: For NRIs, the pitch is simple — a tax-free 7% dollar return from a home-country bank. But the scramble behind the scenes shows how badly India needs the diaspora's savings right now, and how the fine print decides who actually benefits.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: Half of America's Motels Have an Indian Owner. San Francisco Is Building Them a Museum.
nri-world.excerpt: The Tenderloin Museum's permanent Indo-American Hotelier exhibit fixes a diaspora folk fact into history — names, ledgers and all — before the founding generation fades.
nri-world.image_caption: A classic American roadside motel — the kind of property Gujarati immigrant families built into a nationwide hospitality network (Wikimedia Commons)
nri-world.nri_angle: The Patel-motel story is one of the diaspora's most successful but least celebrated immigrant business sagas — a museum claims it as heritage worth preserving rather than a punchline.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: Twenty-Six Years and $8.5 Million Later, a Pennsylvania Temple Opens a School to Outrun Forgetting
nri-world.excerpt: The Bharatiya Learning Center in Chalfont is the diaspora's bet that cultural continuity needs walls, classrooms and a budget — not just good intentions.
nri-world.image_caption: A Hindu temple in the United States, where heritage-language education is taking root in the diaspora (Wikimedia Commons)
nri-world.nri_angle: Every immigrant family negotiates the same bargain: let the kids win in America without becoming strangers to their grandparents. This $8.5M center is that bargain built in brick.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: A 33-Year-Old Indian Newspaper Just Won Australia's Top Multicultural Prize. The Timing Wasn't an Accident.
nri-world.excerpt: Indian Link's fifth Best Multicultural Publication win lands in a year of inflated migration claims and anti-immigration marches — an official counter-signal to louder voices.
nri-world.image_caption: Community-language print media remains one of a diaspora's most durable records of itself (Wikimedia Commons)
nri-world.nri_angle: When mainstream media covers a diaspora only in moments of conflict, the community's own storytellers become its memory — and its defense. This award honors 33 years of that work.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: An H-1B Worker Says He Paid $100,000 to Keep His Job. His Lawsuit Exposes the Visa's Dark Side.
nri-world.excerpt: A Telugu contract worker's labor-trafficking suit in Michigan alleges 'pay-to-stay' exploitation, withheld pay stubs and threats of ICE — a painful mirror for a diaspora that celebrates its own success.
nri-world.image_caption: A federal building and US courthouse; an Indian H-1B worker's labor-trafficking suit is moving through the courts
nri-world.nri_angle: Because the H-1B visa is tied to one employer and Indians face decades-long green-card backlogs, the sponsor holds outsized power — and this lawsuit shows how that power can curdle into forced labor, a warning to the hundreds of thousands of Indians whose American future hangs on a single signature.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: The US Embassy Just Told Indian Visa Holders: The Vetting Never Stops — Even After You're Approved
nri-world.excerpt: A new advisory warns that screening continues after a visa is granted and that 'all available information' stays in play — deepening unease for a community already facing backlogs and 221(g) holds.
nri-world.image_caption: The US Embassy in New Delhi, which has warned that visa screening continues even after a visa is granted
nri-world.nri_angle: For the hundreds of thousands of Indians who enter the US each year on student, work and visitor visas, the embassy's warning reframes an approved visa as a continuously reviewed privilege — raising the stakes on social-media posts, travel and everyday life.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

nri-world.title: 40% of Indian Americans Have Thought About Leaving the US. The 'Reverse Brain Drain' Just Got Its Numbers.
nri-world.excerpt: A Carnegie Endowment survey of 1,000 Indian Americans finds a community in 'turbulence' — with frustration over politics, cost of living and safety driving even successful professionals to weigh the exit.
nri-world.image_caption: Travellers at an airport terminal; nearly 40% of Indian Americans say they have considered leaving the US
nri-world.nri_angle: For 5.2 million people of Indian origin in the US, a survey showing 40% have considered leaving puts hard data to a private unease about belonging — and signals a possible realignment of talent between the country that drew them and the India now courting them back.
nri-world.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: After a Record Exodus, Foreign Investors Tiptoed Back Into Indian Stocks This Week
markets-finance.excerpt: Foreign portfolio investors bought a net ₹1,209 crore of Indian equities in the week to June 20 — a small but symbolically important turn after dumping a record $30 billion-plus through 2026, as a US-Iran peace deal and cheaper oil revived appetite for emerging markets.
markets-finance.image_caption: Foreign investors turned net buyers of Indian equities in the week to June 20 after a record 2026 sell-off
markets-finance.nri_angle: Many NRIs hold Indian equities directly or through mutual funds and India-focused ETFs abroad, so a tentative reversal in foreign flows — the single biggest swing factor for Indian stocks this year — matters directly to diaspora portfolios and to anyone weighing whether the worst of 2026's sell-off is behind them.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: Foreign Money Fled India in April, but a Record Surge in NRI Remittances Helped Cushion the Blow
markets-finance.excerpt: India's balance of payments slipped into a $6.6 billion deficit as portfolio investors pulled out, yet net transfers from overseas Indians jumped to $16 billion — and the RBI's push to draw NRI dollars may turn the tide next year.
markets-finance.image_caption: India's balance of payments slipped into deficit in April even as NRI remittances surged to a record $16 billion
markets-finance.nri_angle: This is the diaspora's economic footprint laid bare: as foreign funds fled Indian stocks, it was the money sent home by Indians working abroad — a record $16 billion in a single month — that helped steady the national accounts, underscoring how central NRIs have become to India's financial stability.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: Jio Files for India's Biggest-Ever IPO — and for the First Time, the Diaspora Can Own a Piece of It
markets-finance.excerpt: Mukesh Ambani's Jio Platforms has filed papers for a Mumbai listing aiming to raise around $3.8 billion, eclipsing every IPO India has seen. For NRIs who use Jio to call home, the company they rely on is about to become one they can invest in.
markets-finance.image_caption: The Bombay Stock Exchange in Mumbai; Jio Platforms has filed for what would be India’s largest-ever IPO, aiming to raise around $3.8 billion
markets-finance.nri_angle: Jio is the invisible infrastructure of diaspora life — the SIM in a parent's phone, the data behind every video call home, the connection that keeps NRI families tethered to India. Now the company behind it is filing for the country's largest-ever IPO, turning a service the diaspora depends on into an asset it can, for the first time, actually own a share of.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: NRIs Are Breaking Their Own Bank Deposits to Chase a Better Rate — and Banks Want the RBI's Blessing
markets-finance.excerpt: A new scheme pays NRIs up to 7.1 percent on dollar deposits, but only on fresh money. Those who locked in months ago at half that rate are now paying penalties to break and rebook — and lenders fear $1 billion could walk out the door.
markets-finance.image_caption: US and Indian currency; NRIs are breaking old dollar deposits to rebook at sharply higher rates
markets-finance.nri_angle: This is a pure diaspora money story: it is NRIs who hold these dollar deposits, NRIs being courted by the new higher rates, and NRIs now weighing whether to pay a penalty to break an old deposit and rebook — a decision facing anyone in the community who parked dollars in an Indian bank in the past year.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: India's Banks Want to Lend You the Dollars to Deposit With Them — and GIFT City Is the Catch
markets-finance.excerpt: Lenders are pressing the RBI to let their GIFT City branches finance the diaspora dollar-deposit scheme designed to shore up the rupee. Nomura reckons the plan could pull in $55 billion — most of it from NRIs — with the bulk arriving by September.
markets-finance.image_caption: Indian and US currency; banks want to fund the RBI's diaspora dollar-deposit scheme via GIFT City branches
markets-finance.nri_angle: This entire scheme is built around the diaspora's dollars — it is NRIs the RBI is trying to coax into Indian banks to defend the rupee — so the mechanics of how banks fund it, and the leverage being negotiated behind the scenes, directly shape the returns and risks facing any overseas Indian weighing an FCNR deposit this summer.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: Indians Pulled Back From the Stock Market in May — but Their Monthly SIPs Hit a Record Anyway
markets-finance.excerpt: Equity mutual fund inflows fell 40 percent to a 12-month low as global jitters spooked lump-sum investors, yet automated SIP contributions climbed to an all-time high of ₹26,688 crore — a sign of how deeply disciplined investing has taken root.
markets-finance.image_caption: Indian rupee notes; monthly SIP contributions hit a record even as equity fund inflows slumped in May
markets-finance.nri_angle: For NRIs who invest in Indian mutual funds through SIPs to stay financially anchored to home, the data is reassuring: India's market is now propped up by steady domestic discipline rather than fickle foreign money, meaning the rupee-cost-averaging strategy many diaspora investors quietly run every month is exactly the behaviour holding the market up.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: India's Five-Day Market Rally Just Snapped — and It Was the IT Giants That Broke It.
markets-finance.excerpt: The Sensex and Nifty slid on Friday as the Nifty IT index crashed to a three-year low, dragged down by an Accenture warning that has put Infosys, Wipro and TCS squarely in investors' crosshairs.
markets-finance.image_caption: An Indian stock-market display; the Sensex and Nifty fell as IT stocks slid to a three-year low
markets-finance.nri_angle: Indian IT is the diaspora's most personal trade — many NRIs work for or hold shares in Infosys, TCS, Wipro and Accenture itself, and a three-year low in the IT index driven by cautious US client spending speaks directly to both their portfolios and their job security in the tech corridors of New Jersey, Texas and the Bay Area.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: Cheaper Oil Should Be Lifting the Rupee. India's Own Central Bank Is Quietly Holding It Back.
markets-finance.excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India's short-dollar forward book has ballooned to a record near $110 billion, and unwinding it — along with hedging the dollars Indian banks are now borrowing abroad — is set to cap the rupee's recovery even as oil sits at three-month lows. For NRIs, it explains why the currency has steadied near 94.5 rather than surged.
markets-finance.image_caption: Indian rupee currency; the RBI's record forward book is set to cap the rupee's recovery despite cheaper oil
markets-finance.nri_angle: NRIs watching the rupee to time remittances, deposits and Indian investments need to understand why a clear tailwind — cheap oil — is not translating into a stronger currency: the RBI's record forward-book overhang means dollar inflows are being absorbed to rebuild reserves rather than allowed to lift the rupee.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: India's Banks Are Rushing to Borrow Dollars Abroad — and the RBI Just Made It Cheaper to Do So
markets-finance.excerpt: HDFC Bank, State Bank of India and Bank of Baroda are all tapping the overseas dollar-bond market this month, the first to use a new Reserve Bank facility that subsidises the cost of hedging foreign borrowing. Bankers expect $15–20 billion to flow in over the next six months — a deliberate effort to defend the rupee and pull in foreign capital.
markets-finance.image_caption: Indian rupee currency; India's banks are raising dollars overseas under a new RBI subsidised hedging window
markets-finance.nri_angle: NRIs hold a direct stake in the rupee's stability — through remittances, NRE/FCNR deposits and Indian bank shares — and this coordinated push to draw dollars into the banking system is one of the clearest signs of how hard New Delhi is working to steady the currency and fund the economy's growth.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: The World's Biggest Investors Are Pouring Billions Into India's Data Centres — the Quiet Backbone of the AI Boom
markets-finance.excerpt: Canada's national pension fund just committed $740 million to an Indian data-centre operator, Apple supplier Jabil teamed up with Adani to build AI hardware in the country, and more than $50 billion of digital-infrastructure spending is now in the pipeline. As global capital races to build the physical plumbing of artificial intelligence, India is emerging as a favoured destination — and a fresh theme for NRI investors.
markets-finance.image_caption: Inside a data centre; global investors are pouring billions into India's data-centre capacity to power the AI boom
markets-finance.nri_angle: Many NRIs work in the very technology and finance industries driving the global AI build-out, and want exposure to India's growth story beyond real estate and fixed deposits; the data-centre boom — backed by the world's largest pension funds and conglomerates — is becoming one of the most investable expressions of that story.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: India Just Cleared the Way for Banks to Pay NRIs More on Their Deposits — But Only Until September.
markets-finance.excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India has temporarily scrapped the interest-rate ceilings on fresh FCNR(B) and longer-tenure NRE deposits through September 30, freeing banks to compete for overseas money as New Delhi scrambles to defend a battered rupee.
markets-finance.image_caption: Indian currency; the RBI has lifted rate caps on select NRI deposits until September 30 to attract overseas funds
markets-finance.nri_angle: This is one of the most directly actionable moves for NRIs all year: with rate caps lifted on FCNR(B) and long NRE deposits until September 30, banks are about to compete for diaspora dollars — meaning the rates Indians abroad earn on parked savings could jump, but only inside a closing window.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

markets-finance.title: India Just Made It Easier for NRIs to Buy Indian Stocks — RBI Opens a New Repatriable Rupee Account
markets-finance.excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India has amended its foreign-exchange rules to let individuals living abroad open dedicated repatriable rupee accounts for investing in listed Indian shares, with sale proceeds free to be sent back overseas. A new 'Individual Foreign Investor' category streamlines the long-tangled plumbing of cross-border equity investment.
markets-finance.image_caption: The Reserve Bank of India has amended its foreign-exchange rules to ease how individuals abroad invest in listed Indian shares
markets-finance.nri_angle: Millions of NRIs want a stake in India's growth story but have long been deterred by a maze of account types, custodial rules and repatriation friction; this RBI amendment is aimed squarely at them, simplifying how a person abroad can buy Indian shares and — just as importantly — get their money back out.
markets-finance.author: Diaspora Desk

sports.title: Jaiswal's Unbeaten 110 Seals a 3-0 Sweep — and the First Clean Verdict on India's Post-Kohli ODI Team
sports.excerpt: India brushed Afghanistan aside by nine wickets in Chennai to complete a whitewash, but the real story is a new-look side under Shubman Gill building quietly toward the 2027 World Cup.
sports.image_caption: Yashasvi Jaiswal, whose unbeaten 110 sealed India's 3-0 ODI series sweep of Afghanistan in Chennai
sports.nri_angle: The Afghanistan sweep is the first full look at India's post-Kohli ODI side under new captain Shubman Gill, whose names — Jaiswal, Kishan, Prasidh Krishna — will headline the white-ball tours bringing India to grounds across North America and England in the years ahead.

sports.title: India Has Never Played a World Cup. On Sunday in Vancouver, a Punjabi From Auckland Carries Its Hopes Anyway.
sports.excerpt: Sarpreet Singh, whose parents left Jalandhar for New Zealand, has become the first Sikh footballer to play at a World Cup — and the Kiwis' must-win clash with Egypt is now appointment viewing for the diaspora.
sports.image_caption: Sarpreet Singh, the New Zealand midfielder of Punjabi heritage who has become the first Sikh footballer to play at a World Cup
sports.nri_angle: India have never played a men's World Cup, but Sarpreet Singh — an Auckland-born midfielder whose parents emigrated from Jalandhar, Punjab — has become the first Sikh footballer to play at one, and his New Zealand side's must-win clash with Egypt makes the tournament personal for South Asian fans across North America.

sports.title: Two Indian-Americans Made the U.S. Open Weekend. Three Recent Champions Did Not.

sports.image_caption: Akshay Bhatia, who made the cut at the 2026 U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills

sports.title: The Bay Area's Team Began Its Season 117 for 2 — and Still Lost. The Unicorns' Collapse Handed LA the Opener.

sports.title: Six Goals, Zero Conceded: India's Women Storm Into the Nations Cup Final — and to the Brink of the Pro League

sports.title: Neeraj Chopra Finished Fourth on His Comeback. The Number That Matters Is 85.69.

sports.image_caption: Neeraj Chopra, who returned from a back injury to finish fourth at the 2026 Doha Diamond League
sports.nri_angle: Neeraj Chopra is the rare Indian track-and-field superstar the diaspora has made appointment viewing, and his healthy return from a long injury lay-off — with a Commonwealth Games berth already secured — keeps alive the medal hopes NRIs rally behind at every global championship.

sports.title: An Ankle Twisted in the Powerplay Ended One World Cup. It Began Another for an Uncapped Spinner Who Was Already in England.
sports.excerpt: Shreyanka Patil is out of the Women's T20 World Cup after injuring her ankle against the Netherlands. Her replacement, 24-year-old legspinner Prema Rawat, has never played for India — and got the call while on an India A tour bus in England.
sports.image_caption: India's women's cricket team with the 2025 Women's Cricket World Cup trophy
sports.nri_angle: India's women's cricket team became a unifying obsession for NRIs after the 2025 50-over World Cup title, and the squad's depth — an uncapped spinner stepping in for an injured star without missing a beat — is exactly the kind of story the diaspora rallies behind as the team chases its first T20 World Cup.

sports.title: He Was Born in Paris, His Mother Is Congolese, and His Tamil Roots Run Through a Caribbean Island. Meet the Fourth Indian at This World Cup.
sports.excerpt: Samuel Moutoussamy played all 90 minutes of DR Congo's 1-1 draw with Portugal in Houston — the least-known of the four players carrying Indian heritage onto the 2026 World Cup stage, and the one with the longest, strangest journey home to it.
sports.image_caption: DR Congo midfielder Samuel Moutoussamy, of Tamil-Guadeloupean and Congolese descent, one of four players of Indian origin at the 2026 World Cup
sports.nri_angle: Samuel Moutoussamy is the fourth and least-known player of Indian descent at the 2026 World Cup — and the one with the deepest diaspora thread, tracing his Tamil roots to 19th-century indentured migrants in the French Caribbean island of Guadeloupe. For a diaspora that has never seen India reach a World Cup, he is an unlikely point of connection, and his June 27 group game against Uzbekistan in Atlanta will be within reach of America's South Asian community.

technology.image_caption: Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, photographed in 2023

technology.excerpt: IBM's Indian-American CEO says fault-tolerant quantum computing arrives by 2029 — and is staking the company's relevance, and a slice of U.S. tech strategy, on getting there first.
technology.image_caption: IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna, photographed in 2025
technology.nri_angle: Arvind Krishna is steering a piece of U.S. national tech strategy, and quantum is one of the few frontiers where the talent pool is still forming rather than being automated — a scarcity bet for diaspora engineers.

technology.title: America Restricted Its Best AI Models. India's Answer Is a Scramble to Build Its Own.

technology.nri_angle: Sovereign AI changes the return-to-India calculus for diaspora engineers and opens an emerging investment class for NRIs — but the 'sovereign' label can outrun revenue, so the fine print matters.

technology.title: Micron Heads Into Earnings With a Memory Shortage So Tight Even Apple Is Flinching

technology.image_caption: Micron Technology chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra, photographed in 2025
technology.nri_angle: Micron's Indian-origin CEO is building a $2.75 billion assembly plant in Gujarat, and the same memory crunch lifting his stock is about to raise prices on every device Indian American families buy.

technology.title: Tim Cook Says Apple's Price Hikes Are 'Unavoidable.' His Successor Inherits the Bill.
technology.excerpt: A memory-chip crunch is forcing Apple to raise prices just as John Ternus prepares to take over in September — and Indian American buyers will feel it first.
technology.image_caption: Apple chief executive Tim Cook, who steps down on September 1, 2026
technology.nri_angle: Apple devices are aspirational status objects in many Indian American homes, and a memory-driven price hike of up to $270 on the next iPhone lands just as a longtime hardware engineer takes the CEO seat.

technology.title: India's Court Backs the Telegram Ban. For 150 Million Users, the Precedent Is the Real Story.
technology.excerpt: A Delhi court upheld a temporary block of Telegram over a medical-exam leak — handing Modi's government a powerful new tool and unsettling a diaspora that lives on the app.
technology.image_caption: The Telegram app icon displayed on a smartphone screen
technology.nri_angle: Telegram is a lifeline for NRIs coordinating family groups, community networks and business across borders; a court endorsing a government shutdown of an entire platform raises the stakes for everyone who relies on Indian internet access.

technology.title: Nikesh Arora Is Buying the Whole Security Stack. The Bill Is Already Past $28 Billion.
technology.excerpt: Palo Alto Networks just closed its $3.3 billion Chronosphere deal weeks after swallowing CyberArk for $25 billion. For the Indians who fill its engineering ranks, the consolidation is the career.
technology.image_caption: Palo Alto Networks chairman and CEO Nikesh Arora speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt
technology.nri_angle: Palo Alto Networks, run by Indian-origin CEO Nikesh Arora, is consolidating the cybersecurity industry around AI agents — reshaping the job market for the thousands of Indian engineers who staff security teams in Santa Clara, Bengaluru and beyond.

technology.excerpt: The Snapdragon maker is in talks to buy AI-chip startup Tenstorrent days before an investor day where it will lay out a data-centre plan. For the Indian engineers who power Qualcomm, the pivot is personal.
technology.image_caption: Qualcomm's headquarters in La Jolla, California; the chipmaker is reportedly spending $10 billion to challenge Nvidia (Wikimedia Commons)
technology.nri_angle: Qualcomm employs thousands of Indian engineers across Hyderabad, Bengaluru and San Diego; its bet to leap from phone chips into AI data-centre silicon decides what those engineers build next — and whether India's chip-design talent gets a seat at the AI hardware table.

technology.title: India's Chip Bet Has a Quiet Winner: A Bengaluru Startup Making the 'Power Brain' for AI Data Centres
technology.excerpt: Peak XV just led a $15 million round into C2i, which builds the power-delivery silicon that keeps GPUs alive. It is the part of India's semiconductor story that doesn't need a billion-dollar fab.
technology.image_caption: A silicon wafer; Bengaluru startup C2i is designing power-management chips for AI data centres (Wikimedia Commons)
technology.nri_angle: India's semiconductor mission is mostly about design IP, not fabs — and design-led startups like C2i are where NRI investors and returning engineers can actually get exposure to the chip story without waiting a decade for a factory.

technology.nri_angle: Indians hold the largest share of H-1B visas, and a layoff triggers a brutal 60-day deadline to find a new sponsor or leave the US — making the 2026 AI-driven cuts an existential threat, not just a career setback.

lifestyle-health.title: Hormone Therapy May Quietly Be Protecting Older Women's Bones, a New Study Finds
lifestyle-health.excerpt: Postmenopausal women on hormone therapy were about 69 percent less likely to have low bone density in their hips and spine, according to research presented at the Endocrine Society's annual meeting — a reminder that menopause reshapes the skeleton long before any fracture.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: Researchers found postmenopausal women on hormone therapy had far lower odds of low bone density on DXA scans
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: South Asian women tend to reach lower peak bone mass and develop osteoporosis at younger ages and lower body weights than many other groups, yet hormone therapy remains stigmatised and under-discussed in many Indian families — making this fresh evidence on its skeletal benefits especially relevant for NRI women navigating menopause far from extended family support.
lifestyle-health.author: Diaspora Desk

lifestyle-health.title: Carrying Extra Weight Does Not Just Raise Dementia Risk — It May Directly Cause It, a Study of 500,000 People Finds
lifestyle-health.excerpt: Using a genetics-based method that mimics a randomised trial, researchers concluded that high body weight and high blood pressure are not merely warning signs but direct causes of vascular dementia — making them, in the authors' words, an “unexploited opportunity” for prevention.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: A study of more than 500,000 people linked high BMI and blood pressure directly to vascular dementia risk
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: South Asians carry abdominal fat and develop high blood pressure and diabetes at lower body-mass thresholds than other populations, often a decade earlier — so a study identifying excess weight and hypertension as direct, modifiable causes of dementia speaks straight to a diaspora that already lives with elevated cardiometabolic risk.
lifestyle-health.author: Diaspora Desk

lifestyle-health.title: Testosterone Alone Won't Fix Diabetes Risk in Older Men, a New Follow-Up Finds — the Lifestyle Still Has to Change
lifestyle-health.excerpt: A long-running Australian trial found that testosterone can improve body composition, blood sugar and libido in older men with belly fat and prediabetes — but only when paired with diet and exercise, not as a shortcut around them.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: A long-running trial found testosterone aids diabetes-risk reduction only alongside diet and exercise, not as a substitute
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: South Asian men carry an outsized burden of type 2 diabetes and abdominal obesity, often at lower body weights than other groups — and as testosterone therapy is marketed ever more aggressively to middle-aged NRIs, this study is a timely reminder that there is no hormonal shortcut around diet and exercise.
lifestyle-health.author: Diaspora Desk

lifestyle-health.title: Hormone-Disrupting Chemicals Are Turning Up in Breast Milk and Babies' Urine, a New Study Finds
lifestyle-health.excerpt: Researchers who tested 336 mother-infant pairs found BPA, phthalates, parabens and pesticides in breast milk and in infants' bodies through their first six months — a reminder that everyday products carry hidden chemical passengers.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: A study of 336 mother-infant pairs detected BPA, phthalates and parabens in breast milk and infant urine
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: Young diaspora families juggling plastic food containers, imported cosmetics and personal-care products will want to read this carefully — the chemicals the study tracked are common in exactly the everyday items that fill NRI households, and the researchers stress this is a call to reduce exposure, not to stop breastfeeding.
lifestyle-health.author: Diaspora Desk

lifestyle-health.title: Cutting Sugar Out Completely May Backfire on Your Gut, a New Study Warns
lifestyle-health.excerpt: Researchers who fed mice a diet with no table sugar at all found their gut bacteria fell out of balance and inflammation rose — a caution for anyone who treats 'zero sugar' as the holy grail of healthy eating.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: A 16-week mouse study found that a totally sucrose-free diet disrupted gut bacteria and raised inflammation
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: Sugar has become the villain in many health-conscious NRI kitchens, where 'no sugar' is now a badge of discipline — but this research suggests that scrubbing sucrose out entirely, rather than simply eating less of it, may quietly unsettle the gut.
lifestyle-health.author: Diaspora Desk

lifestyle-health.title: A Drug Designed to Mend Broken Hearts May Also Heal Damaged Kidneys, Early Research Suggests
lifestyle-health.excerpt: An experimental UCLA compound built to help hearts recover after a heart attack appears to repair injured kidney tissue too — a tantalising prospect for the millions of South Asians living with both heart and kidney disease.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: UCLA's experimental drug AD-NP1, designed to repair heart tissue, also healed injured kidneys in mice
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: South Asians carry a famously high burden of both heart disease and chronic kidney disease — conditions that often travel together with diabetes — so a single drug that might help repair both organs is exactly the kind of breakthrough that could one day matter in NRI households.
lifestyle-health.author: Diaspora Desk

lifestyle-health.title: That Long Afternoon Nap May Be Quietly Stressing a Diabetic's Liver, a New Study Warns
lifestyle-health.excerpt: Researchers tracking people with type 2 diabetes found that daytime naps longer than 30 minutes were linked to a higher risk of fatty liver disease — and combined with poor night sleep, the risk more than tripled.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: A study of people with type 2 diabetes linked daytime naps over 30 minutes to higher fatty-liver risk
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: The afternoon nap is woven into Indian family life — the post-lunch 'aaram' is practically a cultural institution — even as type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease run rampant through the community. A study suggesting that long naps may be quietly raising liver-disease risk in diabetics speaks directly to a habit most NRI households never think twice about.
lifestyle-health.author: Diaspora Desk

lifestyle-health.title: Two Hours of Lifting a Week Cut Women's Heart-Attack Risk by 44 Percent, a Harvard Study of 117,000 Women Finds
lifestyle-health.excerpt: A new analysis in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology followed women for decades and found that resistance training delivered outsized protection against heart disease — a finding with particular weight for South Asian women, who face heart trouble earlier and harder.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: A Harvard study of 117,000 women found two hours of resistance training a week cut heart-attack risk by 44%
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: South Asian women carry an elevated, often under-recognised risk of heart disease, yet strength training remains culturally coded as a man's pursuit in many Indian families. A landmark study showing that just two hours of lifting a week slashes women's heart-attack risk speaks directly to a community where the gym is rarely seen as a place for mothers and aunties — and where the cost of that gap is measured in early heart disease.
lifestyle-health.author: Diaspora Desk

lifestyle-health.title: Ozempic's Active Ingredient May Quietly Be Protecting Bones, a Study of 60,000 Diabetics Finds
lifestyle-health.excerpt: Stanford researchers comparing semaglutide against other weight-loss drugs in people with type 2 diabetes found a 15 percent lower fracture risk — a reassuring twist for a community where diabetes is rampant and bones are already thinner.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: A semaglutide injection pen; a study of 60,000 diabetics linked the drug to 15% fewer fractures
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: Indians are among the most diabetes-prone people on earth and tend to have lower bone density than Western populations, so a finding that a wildly popular weight-loss drug many NRIs are already taking may also guard against fractures speaks directly to two health risks the diaspora carries at once.
lifestyle-health.author: Diaspora Desk

lifestyle-health.title: A Non-Hormone Pill for Menopause Just Passed Its First Real-World Test — on Hot Flashes and Mood Alike
lifestyle-health.excerpt: In a study of 656 women, the FDA-approved drug fezolinetant eased hot flashes, night sweats, anxiety and depression within weeks — an option that matters for the many South Asian women who avoid or cannot take hormone therapy.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: A study of 656 women found the non-hormone drug fezolinetant eased hot flashes and mood within weeks
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: Menopause remains a taboo, under-treated subject in many Indian families, and cultural wariness about hormone therapy leaves countless diaspora women suffering in silence — so evidence that a non-hormonal pill measurably eases hot flashes, sleep loss and mood is exactly the kind of option that could reach women who would never consider hormones.
lifestyle-health.author: Diaspora Desk

lifestyle-health.title: The Smartwatch on Your Wrist May Be Quietly Doing Your Heart a Favour, a Review of 14 Trials Finds
lifestyle-health.excerpt: Pooling 14 clinical trials, researchers found that heart-disease patients who used fitness apps or wearables walked nearly 1,100 more steps a day than those who did not — a small, low-cost nudge with outsized relevance for a community that develops heart disease early.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: A fitness tracker; a review of 14 trials found heart patients using such tools walked about 1,100 more steps daily
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: People of Indian origin suffer heart attacks up to a decade earlier than other populations and are among the most enthusiastic adopters of smartwatches and fitness rings — so the finding that a device many NRIs already wear can measurably push them to move more turns a gadget on the wrist into a genuine, low-cost cardiac-prevention tool for the diaspora.
lifestyle-health.author: Diaspora Desk

lifestyle-health.title: A Head Injury Can Raise the Risk of Brain Disease. New Research Says the Danger May Run Both Ways.
lifestyle-health.excerpt: A study of more than 55,000 older veterans finds that those recently diagnosed with stroke, dementia, epilepsy or Parkinson's were far more likely to have suffered a traumatic brain injury — a finding that reframes fall prevention as brain protection for ageing parents.
lifestyle-health.image_caption: An older adult walking with support; falls are the main cause of traumatic brain injury in the elderly
lifestyle-health.nri_angle: Millions of NRIs are caring for ageing parents — some living abroad with them, many supporting elders back in India from a distance — and this research delivers a sharp, actionable warning: a parent newly diagnosed with dementia, stroke, epilepsy or Parkinson's is in a high-risk window for a fall-related head injury, making home fall-proofing one of the most concrete things a diaspora family can do.
